title: Scientists Report Blood Traces in a 115-Million-Year-Old Dinosaur Bone
paragraphs: A Curtin University-led team contends that the limb bones of a 115-million-year-old theropod from northeastern Brazil, Aratasaurus museunacionali, retain chemical fingerprints of blood, a claim that, should it withstand scrutiny, would stretch accepted assumptions about how long fragile biomolecules can endure. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The authors describe numerous mineralised red blood cells lodged in the vascular canals and report heme, the oxygen-binding unit of hemoglobin, alongside amino acids associated with collagen. Their account credits hausmannite, a manganese-rich mineral that seems to have enveloped the cells and held them in a kind of geochemical stasis. Lead author Professor Kliti Grice has called the result "a landmark discovery".

Yet prudence is warranted. The proposed sequence, in which the carcass was swiftly entombed in oxygen-starved, microbe-laden sediment, is the researchers' conjecture rather than an established mechanism, and the entire case rests on a single specimen. Reports of preserved dinosaur soft tissue have long been a bone of contention, so independent replication will ultimately decide whether this is a turning point or merely another contested claim. Funding came from a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Grice; the suggested relevance to the search for life beyond Earth remains, for now, conjecture.

questions.q: What is the central claim of the study?
questions.a: That a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone still holds chemical traces of blood.

questions.q: What do the authors credit for the preservation?
questions.a: A manganese-rich mineral, hausmannite, plus rapid burial in oxygen-poor sediment.
It rests on one specimen and earlier soft-tissue claims were disputed.
